newsitem.title: UK: Ratings bode well for Moscow Eurobond plans.
newsitem.headline: Ratings bode well for Moscow Eurobond plans.

text.p: Moscow city's plans to raise money through its first international debt issue received a boost on Monday after it was awarded high speculative grade credit ratings, bankers said.
"They are pretty respectable ratings, and the agencies said they were constrained by Russia's sovereign ceiling," a Eurobond trader at a European bank said.
"It is quite significant they specifically said this, and is an indication Moscow is a strong credit. This could help with the pricing (of its Eurobond)," he said.

Moody's Investors Service on Monday said it would rate the City of Moscow's forthcoming Eurobond issue Ba2. It said the rating was constrained by the Russian Federation's existing Ba2 foreign-currency rating.
Later, Standard & Poor's assigned Moscow's foreign currency debt a BB minus rating, and also said it was constrained by Russia's sovereign ceiling.

While a sovereign ceiling represents the highest foreign debt credit rating that a borrower in the country can receive, bankers said the agencies' specific reference to the constraint implied the credit rating could even have been higher.
Moscow, together with other Russian cities like St Petersburg, has been preparing to raise money on the international capital markets since last year.
The next expected rating news from the region is for St Petersburg, which dealers said was also likely to receive the same ratings as Russia.

"St Petersburg is a fairly strong credit which is also expected to get the sovereign ceiling. But whether or not the rating agencies say they were constrained by the sovereign ceiling is another question and will be interesting to see," the Eurobond trader said.

Last week, Moscow city officials said a $400 million Eurobond would be launched by March 15. The deal, which will be underwritten by Credit Suisse First Boston and Nomura, is expected to have a three- or five-year maturity, dealers said.
Russia tapped the Eurobond market for the first time since the 1917 revolution when it launched a $1.0 billion five-year bond last November.
Priced to yield 345 basis points over U.S. Treasury notes, the paper was trading at 330 b.p. over on Monday.
"Moscow is planning a much smaller deal, and today's ratings could help with the pricing," a syndicate manager covering Russian Eurobonds said.
"If Moscow opts for a three-year bond they will price relative to Kazakhstan's outstanding three-year deal which is trading at around 250 b.p. over Treasuries," he said.
Kazakhstan is rated Ba3 by Moody's and BB minus by S&P.

A major obstacle to Eurobond issues from Russian municipalities was overcome last Friday when first deputy prime minister Vladimir Potanin said deals would not be subject to a 15 percent government security tax.
Russia had also decided to drop a proposal to charge an 0.8 percent fee for registering Eurobonds, he said.
In addition to Moscow and St Petersburg, Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region is also preparing a debut Eurobond issue
